{{Short description|Example of a topology on the set of positive integers}}
In [[general topology]], a branch of mathematics, the '''Appert topology''', named for {{harvs|txt|last=Appert|first=Antoine|year=1934}}, is a [[topological space|topology]] on the set {{nowrap|1=''X'' = {1, 2, 3, ...}}} of [[natural number|positive integers]].<ref name="CEIT">{{harvnb|Steen|Seebach|1995|pp=117–118}}</ref>
In the Appert topology, the open sets are those that do not contain 1, and those that asymptotically contain almost every positive integer.  The space ''X'' with the Appert topology is called the '''Appert space'''.<ref name="CEIT"/>

== Construction ==

For a subset ''S'' of ''X'', let {{nowrap|1=N(''n'',''S'')}} denote the number of elements of ''S'' which are less than or equal to ''n'':
:<math> \mathrm{N}(n,S) = \#\{ m \in S : m \le n \} . </math>

''S'' is defined to be open in the Appert topology if either it does not contain 1 or if it has [[asymptotic density]] equal to 1, i.e., it satisfies
:<math>\lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{\text{N}(n,S)}{n} = 1</math>.

The empty set is open because it does not contain 1, and the whole set ''X'' is open since
<math>\text{N}(n,X)/n=1</math> for all ''n''.

== Related topologies ==
The Appert topology is closely related to the [[Fort space]] topology that arises from giving the set of integers greater than one the [[discrete topology]], and then taking the point 1 as the point at infinity in a [[one point compactification]] of the space.<ref name="CEIT"/>  The Appert topology is finer than the Fort space topology, as any cofinite subset of ''X'' has asymptotic density equal to 1.

==Properties==
* The closed subsets ''S'' of ''X'' are those that either  contain 1 or that have zero asymptotic density, namely <math>\lim_{n\to\infty} \mathrm{N}(n,S)/n = 0</math>.
* Every point of ''X'' has a [[local basis]] of [[clopen sets]], i.e., ''X'' is a [[zero-dimensional space]].<ref name="CEIT"/><br>''Proof'': Every open neighborhood of 1 is also closed.  For any <math>x\ne 1</math>, <math>\{x\}</math> is both closed and open.
* ''X'' is [[Hausdorff space|Hausdorff]] and [[perfectly normal space|perfectly normal]] (T<sub>6</sub>).<br>''Proof'': ''X'' is T<sub>1</sub>.  Given any two disjoint closed sets ''A'' and ''B'', at least one of them, say ''A'', does not contain 1.  ''A'' is then clopen and ''A'' and its complement are disjoint respective neighborhoods of ''A'' and ''B'', which shows that ''X'' is normal and Hausdorff.  Finally, any subset, in particular any closed subset, in a countable T<sub>1</sub> space is a G<sub>δ</sub>, so ''X'' is perfectly normal.
* ''X'' is countable, but not [[first countable]],<ref name="CEIT"/> and hence not [[second countable]] and not [[metrizable]].
* A subset of ''X'' is [[compact space|compact]] if and only if it is finite.  In particular, ''X'' is not [[locally compact space|locally compact]], since there is no compact neighborhood of 1.
* ''X'' is not [[countably compact]].<ref name="CEIT"/><br>''Proof:'' The infinite set <math>\{2^n:n\ge 1\}</math> has zero asymptotic density, hence is closed in ''X''.  Each of its points is isolated.  Since ''X'' contains an infinite closed discrete subset, it is not [[limit point compact]], and therefore it is not countably compact.
